title: 5 signs of a fabricated CV
body: 1. Overlapping full-time roles — line up the month/year of every job. Two full-time jobs rarely run in parallel.
2. Impossible tenure — '12 years of leadership' with a 2018 graduation date.
3. Senior titles at tiny companies — check headcount on the company page before you trust 'VP'.
4. CV updated minutes before applying with your exact JD language.
5. References limited to HR or friends, never a direct manager.
takeaway: Build a 30-second 'timeline check' into every screen: dates, headcount, references.

title: Claimed vs demonstrated skills
body: A skill on a CV is a claim; a story with specifics is evidence.
Ask 'what did YOU configure / decide / write?' — consumers of a technology describe it in the passive voice.
Look for artefacts: post-mortems, repos, dashboards, numbers with a baseline.
Candidates who say 'I haven't done that in production' are often more trustworthy than those who claim everything.
takeaway: Replace 'Do you know X?' with 'Tell me about the last time you did X yourself.'

title: When to overrule your AI shortlist
body: AI match scores reward keyword overlap. Polished CVs and JD-mirrored language inflate them.
Overrule when the evidence (interview specifics, references, timeline) contradicts the score.
Don't overrule on gut feel alone — AI is right often, and unnecessary overrules waste good candidates.
Track your overrules: if you're right less than half the time, slow down and gather one more signal.
takeaway: AI shortlists. Humans make the call — with evidence.

title: How college-tier and gap bias shrink your talent pool
body: College tier predicts very little about job performance after the first 2 years of work.
Career gaps (caregiving, health, study) are disproportionately taken by women and carers — penalising them cuts a large qualified pool.
Age signals ('graduated 2002') trigger assumptions about adaptability that the evidence rarely supports.
Blind screening (hide name, photo, institute, age) at the first pass measurably narrows rating gaps.
takeaway: Score the evidence first, then look at the profile. Try a blind first pass on your next role.

title: Reading behavioural signals in interviews
body: Listen for pronouns: 'I' for blame-free wins and 'they' for failures is a red flag; 'we' for wins and 'I' for misses is a green one.
Dismissive language about former teams or managers predicts conflict and attrition.
Ask about failure. Strong candidates own it and describe what they changed.
Confidence isn't competence — calm specifics beat high-energy slogans.
takeaway: Always ask one 'tell me about a time you failed' question and score ownership.

title: Matching sourcing channels to the role
body: Volume and junior roles: job boards, referrals and AI sourcing agents — fast and cheap.
Senior engineers: communities, GitHub and referrals — the best ones are passive.
Leadership: referrals, internal successors and (if budget allows) exec search.
Measure cost-per-hire AND 6-month quality by channel, not just applicant volume.
takeaway: Pick channels by where the best candidates already are, not where applications are easiest.

title: Why structured interviews cut mis-hires
body: Structured interviews (same questions, scored against anchors) predict performance roughly twice as well as unstructured chats.
Generic questions ('Where do you see yourself in 5 years?') produce rehearsed answers and no new information.
Design each question to test one specific claim or risk you found in the CV.
Write the 'good answer' anchor before the interview, not after.
takeaway: For every CV, write one question that could prove the candidate wrong.

title: Closing offers without breaking the band
body: Know the candidate's real motivator before the number: growth, flexibility, team, or cash.
Non-cash levers (joining bonus, WFH days, learning budget, title clarity) close many gaps.
Meeting in the middle signals respect; holding firm works only when you're clearly the best option.
Walking away is a valid outcome when the ask breaks internal parity.
takeaway: Ask 'What would make this a clear yes?' before you make the offer.

title: Fast is good. Rushed is expensive.
body: Top candidates are off the market in ~10 days — speed matters.
But a bad hire costs 30–150% of annual salary. Speed without verification is a false saving.
Use time-boxes: decide your 'must-verify' list up front, verify it, then move.
Over-deliberation has a cost too: candidates ghost slow processes.
takeaway: Set a must-verify checklist per role so you can move fast with confidence.

title: Rejection is a brand moment
body: Most candidates never hear back — and tell others about it.
A 3-line personalised note (one strength, one reason, one door left open) takes 2 minutes.
Silver-medallists are your cheapest future hires: keep them in a talent pool and stay in touch.
Candidate experience scores correlate with offer acceptance.
takeaway: Never leave a finalist without personal feedback.

title: Calibrate your confidence
body: Over-confident recruiters skip verification; under-confident ones over-interview.
Before each final decision, write your confidence (1–5). Review it against 6-month outcomes.
Good calibration means your 5/5 calls are right ~90% of the time.
takeaway: Keep a decision journal for your next 10 hires.
